Joint Injuries: Sprains, Strains, Subluxations and Dislocations Explained in Details

Joint injuries include sprains, strains, subluxations and dislocations and those will be explained here

Sprain

  • Injury of ligaments and joint capsule
  • Most common locations for sprains are knee, ankle and acromioclavicular joint
  • Mechanism of injury is by twisting or tilting forces affecting the joint

Sprain Grading

Grade Description
Grade 1 Minimal tearing of the ligament. Heals completely without any dysfunction
Grade 2 Partial tearing of the ligament. Can’t heal completely which lead to weakness in the ligament (easy to get injured)
Grade 3 Complete tearing (rupture). Leads to joint instability

Sprain Clinical features

  • Patient reports that the joint suddenly forced into abnormal position after trauma, sometimes patient hears or feels a snap
  • Acute severe pain with/without contusion and hemarthrosis
  • On examination (mostly under anesthesia) you find about joint instability using special tests

Sprain radiographic features

  • Best seen with US and MRI, X ray is normal
  • Injured ligament show the following features
    • Thickened and hypoechoic ligament with area of discontinuity of fibers
    • Edema along the injured ligament
    • Hemorrhage

Sprain treatment

  • Any ligament injury grade treated conservatively initially
  • RICE: resting the injured limb, putting Ice on the injury for less than 20 minutes, compression with a bandage and elevation of the injured limb to limit edema formation
  • The sprained joint supported in a splint, after 1-2 weeks the splint is exchanged for a functional brace to allow joint movement
  • Physiotherapy is initiated to strengthen the muscles around the sprained joint
  • After a while, there is usually some joint instability, if it is symptomatic then surgical reconstruction of the ligament is needed

Strain

  • Strain is an injury to a muscle or a tendon or both
  • Strain is mostly caused as a result of playing sports, usually the tendon or muscle overstretches and injuries
  • Strain could be partial tearing or complete tearing or tendon rupture
  • Strain could be acute (following trauma), or chronic due to repetitive tearing of a muscle or tendon

Strain Clinical features

  • Pain
  • Loss of function of the affected muscle
  • Contusion of the skin overlying the muscle
  • Localized inflammation

Strain classification

Grade Description
Grade 1 mild strain with minimal tearing of muscle fibers or tendon
Grade 2 moderate strain with partial tearing of muscle fibers or tendon
Grade 3 severe strain with completely torn muscle or tendon

Strain treatment

  • Initially strain treated with Resting the injured limb, applying Ice to induce vasoconstriction for less than 20 minutes to limit the edema and contusion formed, Compression of the injured area with bandage and Elevation of the injured limb to limit the edema
  • All those steps are collected in the mnemonic RICE
  • NSAIDs also used to reduce pain and swelling
  • If grade 3 injury of the tendon or muscle, then it should be repaired operatively

Dislocations and subluxations

  • Dislocation is complete displacement between the joint surfaces (no contact)
  • Subluxation is incomplete or partial displacement of the joint surfaces

Dislocations and subluxations clinical features

  • The joint is painful
  • Patient avoid moving it
  • There is obvious deformity of the joint
  • X ray should be done, shows the dislocations and associated bony injury if any

Dislocations and subluxations treatment

  • The dislocation must be reduced as soon as possible
  • Sedation is required, general anesthesia maybe needed
  • Muscle relaxant maybe used
  • After reduction , the joint is rested until soft tissue welling decreases
  • Then controlled movement begin with physiotherapy
  • There might be residual instability or recurrency of the dislocation which is solved by surgery

Dislocations and subluxations complications

  • Vascular injury
  • Nerve injury
  • Avascular necrosis
  • Joint stiffness
  • Osteoarthritis

Loop Diuretics: Types, Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses and Adverse Effects

Types

  • We have four loop diuretics: furosemide (Lasix), bumetanide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid
  • Bumetanide and torsemide are more potent than furosemide
  • Ethacrynic acid has a lot of adverse effects

Pharmacokinetics

  • Furosemide absorption by 60% while bumetanide absorbed by 100%
  • Bumetanide would be more potent than furosemide
  • If taken orally diuresis start after 30 minutes while if taken intravenously the diuresis starts after 5 minutes
  • After absorption they go into different sites of the body including the kidney where they get secreted through the proximal convoluted tubule and then after that they move until they reach the TAL where their site of action located

Mechanism of action

  • Loop diuretics blocks NaKCl in the TAL of loop of Henle
  • Loop diuretics inhibit the cotransport of Na+/K+/2Cl− in the luminal membrane in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle, (NaKCl accounts for reabsorption of 25% to 30% of filtered NaCl)
  • So we would lose na, water, k/cl, mg/ca, H+
  • Loop diuretics enhance prostaglandin E2 and I2 synthesis which lead to renal vasodilation and increase blood flow to kidney Lead to increase GFR
  • And also have systemic vasodilatation effect that would lower the blood pressure
  • Speaking of GFR, loop diuretics can work even if GFR is 10 ml/min (end stage renal failure) and that ‘s why it is called high ceiling diuretics (very efficient)

Therapeutic uses

  • Acute pulmonary edema
    • The loop diuretics are the drugs of choice for reducing acute pulmonary edema and acute/chronic peripheral edema caused from heart failure or renal impairment. Because of their rapid onset of action, particularly when given intravenously, the drugs are useful in emergency situations such as acute pulmonary edema.
    • In people who have left side heart failure and the blood is congested in the lung and also in people who have severe hypertension and their after load is very high due to systemic vasoconstriction
    • The blood going from right ventricle to lungs and then goes back into left ventricle where it cannot be ejected either because left side of heart is weak or either because of systemic vascular resistance
    • This lead to intrapulmonary hydrostatic pressure increase => lung capillaries would leak water and this lead to cyanosis and difficulty breathing => acute pulmonary edema
    • This treated with furosemide injection that lead to decrease volume => decrease after load ; increase PGE2 and I2 that lead to vasodiltation and decrease systemic vascular resistance and blood ejecting from the pulmonary veins and also lead vasodiltation in lungs and congestion relief
  • Acute or chronic peripheral edema
  • Acute or chronic renal failure
    • Loop diuretics can work even if GFR is 10 ml/min (very efficient)
    • It also increase PGE2/I2 => vasodiltation => increase blood flow into kidney => increase GFR
  • Hypertensive emergencies
    • When systolic pressure > 180 => cerebral hemorrhage or encephalopathy
    • Loops diuretics decrease blood pressure by
    • 1- decrease water in the body
    • 2- increase PGE2 and I2 => vasodiltation
    • 3- decrease Na in the body
    • Na make blood vessels endothelium more sensitive to catecholamines which lead to vasoconstriction; so by decreasing it this lead to decrease BP
  • Hypercalcemia
    • Loop diuretics with hydration used for treating hypercalcemia, because they stimulate tubular ca excretion

Adverse effects

  • Acute hypovolemia: Loop diuretics can cause a severe and rapid reduction in blood volume, with the possibility of hypotension, shock, and cardiac arrhythmias
  • Potassium depletion
  • Hypomagnesemia
  • Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
  • Hyperuricemia
  • Disturbed glucose metabolism and hyperlipidemia
  • Ototoxicity
  • Hypersensitivity

Melatonin for Sleep: Mechanism of Action & Side Effects

Melatonin

  • Melatonin is a hormone that is produced by the pineal gland in the brain and its main function is related to regulating sleep- wake cycle and circadian rhythm
  • Darkness triggers melatonin production, which when secreted gives hypnotic effect (sleep effect), light decrease production of the hormone
  • Insomnia became problematic when artificial light was discovered, artificial light decreased melatonin levels
  • In the early 2000s, comes the idea of using this hormone as a medication or a supplement to treat insomnia

Therapeutic Uses

  • Melatonin is used as a supplement for treatment of insomnia and improving sleep
  • It is also used to overcome jet lag
  • REM sleep behavior disorders

Mechanism of action

  • Melatonin act as agonist on melatonin receptors including MT1, MT2 in the hypothalamus to mediate sleep and regulates circadian rhythm

Pharmacokinetics

  • Available as oral formulas only
  • Good absorption with bioavailability of 2- 50%
  • Distribution: melatonin is bound to plasma proteins by 60%
  • It is metabolized by CYP enzymes in the liver and it is liable to be affected by CYP inducers and inhibitors
  • Elimination: 90% eliminated through urine and the rest in bile and elimination half life is about 30 minutes

Side effects

  • Dizziness
  • Fatigue
  • Nausea
  • Exacerbated insomnia
  • Hypertension
  • Abdominal pain
  • Heartburn
  • Mouth ulcers
  • Aggression
  • Pruritus
  • Glycosuria
  • Increased weight
  • Mood swings
  • Tiredness
  • Abnormal liver function test

Contraindications

  • It is contraindicated in Previous hypersensitivity reactions
  • It is not recommended in autoimmune diseases, pregnancy, breastfeeding and liver diseases

Methadone Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

Overview

  • Methadone is a synthetic opioid analgesic medication
  • It was developed in Germany in 1939 by German chemists Gustav Ehrhart and Max Bockemühl
  • Methadone is famous for being used in treatment of opioid dependence

Pharmacokinetics

  • Available in multiple oral formulas, including pills, sublingual tablets and drinkable formulas too
  • Methadone metabolized by liver by CYP2B6 and CYP3A4
  • Methadone is excreted exclusively through bile
  • Half life is long (12- 25 hours) but the duration of analgesia is 4- 8 hours

Mechanism of action

  • Methadone work as agonist on the opioid receptors, especially mu receptors which are available everywhere in the human body, especially the CNS
  • Methadone can also block NMDA receptors and monoaminergic reuptake transporters (both of those are non opioid related receptors), blockage of these receptors explain methadone ability to relieve difficult to treat pain (e.g. neuropathic and cancer pain), when morphine doesn’t work

Pharmacologic Effects

  • Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several central effects (CNS effects):
    • Analgesia: Methadone provide a better analgesia at 10-20% of morphine equivalent dose
    • Euphoria
    • Sedation
    • Respiratory depression
    • Cough suppression
    • Nausea and vomiting
    • Miosis
    • Pruritus due to histamine release
    • Truncal rigidity
  • Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several peripheral effects including:
    • CVS: bradycardia and hypotension
    • GIT: constipation
    • RS: less bronchoconstriction compared to morphine (less histamine release)
    • Urinary system: may lead to urine retention
    • Immune: decrease immunity

Therapeutic uses

  • One of the adverse effects of opioid use is opioid dependence
  • Methadone is widely used in the treatment of opioid dependence, it maybe used as maintenance therapy or in shorter periods to manage withdrawal symptoms
  • Methadone is used to treat opioid dependence for these reasons:
    • Tolerance and physical dependence develop more slowly with methadone than with other opioids due to its long half life
    • After sudden withdrawal of methadone, withdrawal signs and symptoms are milder and prolonged compared to other opioids with shorter half lives withdrawal
  • Another use of methadone is in treatment of chronic pain, it is more effective for neuropathic pain due to its action on NMDA receptors

Methadone maintenance therapy (MMT)

  • Takes place in outpatient settings, methadone prescribed as a single daily dose for those who wish to abstain from illicit opioid use
  • Duration of MMT ranges from few months to years and it maybe life long because opioid dependence characterized by being chronically relapsing and remitting through the patient life
  • The starting doses are not exceeding 40 mg/ daily and then tapered gradually

Adverse effects

  • Respiratory depression
  • Methadone lead to increase QT interval (because of its action of potassium channels in the heart) and may lead to torsade’s de pointes arrhythmia
  • Constipation
  • Sedation
  • Weakness, dizziness and headache
  • Dry mouth
  • Sleep disturbance
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Mild amnesia

Monteggia Fracture Dislocation: Bado Classification, Treatment and Complications

Monteggia fracture dislocation is any fracture of the ulna associated with a radial head dislocation

Monteggia occur more commonly in children and rarely in adults

Diagnosed by forearm X-rays and treated either operatively or non operatively

Mechanism of injury

  • Monteggia result from a fall on the outstretched hand with twisting force or a force that lead to hyperextension of the elbow joint
  • It also can occur from direct blow to the forearm and from high energy injuries

Classification

Classified according to Bado classification

Bado classifies Monteggia fractures according to the direction of the radial head dislocation and the direction of the angulation of the ulna fracture into four types, those include:

  • Type I
  • Type II
  • Type III
  • Type IV
Bado Type Description
Type I Anterior dislocation of the radial head + angulated ulna fracture with the apex pointing anteriorly (most common type 60%)
Type II Posterior dislocation of the radial head + angulated ulna fracture with the apex pointing posteriorly (worst prognosis)
Type III Lateral dislocation of the radial head + ulnar fracture
Type IV dislocation of the radial head in any direction + fractures of both the radius and ulna

Bado Type IV Monteggia fracture; by Benoudina Samir, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Bado Type IV Monteggia fracture; by Benoudina Samir, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Clinical features

Symptoms

  • Patient present with pain in the forearm and elbow

Physical examination

Look

  • Look for Swelling
  • Deformity of the ulna is obvious, but the elbow deformity is masked by swelling
  • Inspect the lacerations for any evidence of open fracture

Feel

  • Feel for tenderness (esp. on the lateral side of the forearm)
  • Neurovascular examination is done to look for nerve/vessel injury (esp. radial nerve)

Move

  • Patient refuse movement due to pain
  • Examination is repeated multiple times to exclude compartment syndrome

Imaging

  • Plain radiographs (AP and lateral) are enough for diagnosis
  • The radiograph should include the elbow and wrist to detect any injuries to the proximal or distal radioulnar joints
  • Radial head is dislocated and does not point to the capitulum anymore (because normally the radius points to the capitulum in all elbow X ray views)
  • Ulnar fracture might by incomplete (greenstick) in children and the radial head is not completely ossified so it can be easily missed on X-rays

Lateral forearm X-ray showing Monteggia fracture dislocation; by Jane Agnes, CC BY-SA 3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Lateral forearm X-ray showing Monteggia fracture dislocation; by Jane Agnes, CC BY-SA 3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Emergency management

  • Grossly displaced fracture should be reduced in the emergency department
  • Above elbow backslab is applied to support the fracture and prevent forearm rotation

Treatment

  • Non operative
  • Operative

Non operative

  • Non operative treatment is done in children for the incomplete fractures only (greenstick fractures)
  • reduction is achieved by restoring the ulna to its normal length by traction
  • Then the forearm is immobilized in above elbow cast for 3 weeks and Re examination is done and radiographs are repeated
  • Exercises are started as soon as possible

Operative

  • Operative treatment is done when ulnar fracture is a complete fractures
  • Operative treatment is achieved with closed reduction of the radial head and ORIF and plating of the ulnar fracture
  • Radial head is reduced by closed reduction, if it remains stable throughout full range of motion of the elbow then no further management needed; but if it re dislocates or it can’t be reduced then it has to be explored and repaired

Complications

Early Complications

  • Nerve injury: mostly iatrogenic happen during reduction or during surgery, and they are mostly neuropraxias that will recover on their own
  • Vascular injury
  • Compartment syndrome

Late Complications

  • Malunion: occur when the ulna is not perfectly reduced which lead to the radial head remains dislocated and limits elbow flexion
  • Non union: treated by plating and bone grafting
  • Elbow stiffness: occur especially when the radial head dislocation is missed and when the elbow is immobilized for a longer period of time

Morphine Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

Overview

  • Morphine is the prototypical opioid, Opioids are analgesic drugs
  • Morphine is derived from the opium plant and isolated in 1803
  • Name morphine is after Morpheus (the Greek god of dreams)

Pharmacokinetics

  • Available as oral, IV, IM and subcutaneous
  • Good oral absorption
  • Bioavailability after oral administration is 25% due to significant first pass effect
  • Distribution: morphine quickly leave the blood and into the tissues mainly brain, lungs, liver, kidneys and spleen
  • Half life is 4-5 hours
  • Metabolized in the liver by conjugation into active and inactive metabolites
  • Excretion 90% through kidneys, 10% through bile

Opioids mechanism of action

  • Morphine work on the opioid receptors which are three major receptors Mu (μ), and delta (δ), kappa (κ)
  • each of these receptors has subtypes, μ has μ 1 and μ 2, δ has δ1 and δ2, κ has κ1 and κ2
  • All of these receptors are G protein coupled receptors
  • These receptors all located everywhere in the body including brain, spinal cord (esp. dorsal horn) and peripheral tissues
  • morphine bind to these receptors and act as agonists on those receptors
  • Morphine exhibit a greater affinity to μ receptors

Morphine pharmacologic effects

  • Activation of these opioid receptors by morphine lead to several central effects (CNS effects):
    • Analgesia
    • Euphoria
    • Sedation
    • Respiratory depression
    • Cough suppression
    • Miosis
    • Nausea and vomiting
    • Pruritus
  • Activation of these opioid receptors by morphine lead to several peripheral effects including:
    • CVS
    • GIT
    • RS
    • Renal
    • Endocrine
    • Immune

Analgesia

  • Dose dependent analgesia, patient stay conscious and can locate the source of the pain
  • Morphine analgesia is sensory and emotional so the patient pain improves if it was due to physical problem or if it was psychological

Morphine analgesic mechanisms

  1. Morphine works on the opioid receptors (mu, kappa, delta) in the posterior horn of the spinal cord, those receptors are located in high densities in the posterior horn and once activated would decrease release of substance P which lead to decrease pain sensation and this is called spinal analgesia
  2. Morphine also work by activating the opioid receptors in the brain which once activated there it would activate the descending inhibitory pain control pathways which also lead to decrease pain sensation, and this is called supraspinal analgesia
  3. Morphine decrease norepinephrine release in the CNS, this lead to decrease the psychological pain
  4. Morphine also work on the peripheral opioid receptors in the painful tissue

Euphoria

  • Pleasant sensation with decrease anxiety
  • People seek this effect during recreational use of this drug
  • Result from decreasing norepinephrine release in some CNS areas

Sedation

  • Decrease consciousness (drowsiness)
  • Some amnesia
  • Sometimes sleep (patient can be easily aroused) in comparison with sedative hypnotics drugs may results in deep sleep

Respiratory depression

  • All the opioids agonists including morphine lead to respiratory depression by inhibiting the respiratory center in the brainstem
  • Dose dependent
  • CO2 retention occurs with cerebral vasodilatation and increase ICP
  • Respiratory depression is worse in patients with asthma, COPD, head trauma

Cough suppression

  • Morphine suppresses cough
  • May lead to accumulation of secretions and atelectasis

Miosis

  • Constriction of the pupils occur with all opioid agonists including Morphine due to vagal stimulation, miosis is when pupil size less than 2 mm
  • Mediated by parasympathetic pathway which can be blocked by atropine
  • Severe miosis is indicative of toxic doses
  • Miosis is a fixed feature in all addicts

Nausea and vomiting

  • Occur due to activation of chemoreceptor trigger zone => nausea and vomiting

Temperature

  • morphine produces hyperthermia through its action on the mu receptors

Morphine aggravate itching

  • Morphine effect decrease pain but not itching, because itching has its own receptors which are different than pain receptors
  • The mechanism of pruritus is through peripheral release of histamine and central activation of pruriceptive neural circuits

CVS system

  • Morphine lead to bradycardia due to vagal stimulation
  • Hypotension may occur with opioid use if there is some pathology in the CVS system
  • Histamine release aid in development of hypotension

Respiratory system

  • Morphine lead to Bronchoconstriction due to
    • vagal stimulation
    • histamine release
  • Morphine also works on mu and delta receptors in the bronchi leading to bronchoconstriction

GIT tract

  • Opioid receptors exist in high density in the GIT, when activation lead to decrease stomach motility and increase the tone ;; HCl secretion decreased
  • Small intestine tone increased with periodic spasms, amplitude of nonpropulsive contractions is decreased
  • Large intestine propulsive peristaltic waves markedly decreased and tone is increased which lead to delay passage of feces and allows more absorption of water which ultimately lead to constipation
  • Constipation is a major problem in opioid use for cancer pain…
  • This can be advantageous in diarrhea treatment, there is opioids that are modified to not cross blood brain barrier so they work on GIT only to treat diarrhea like loperamide

Biliary tract

  • Contraction of biliary smooth muscles => biliary colic
  • Contraction of sphincter of oddi => reflux of biliary and pancreatic secretions

Renal

  • Mu receptors activation in the kidney and CNS have antidiuretic effects and lead to decrease renal function
  • Ureteral and bladder tone are increased and sphincter tones also increased which may lead to urine retention especially in postoperative patients
  • Ureteral colic could become worse when using opioid as a pain control

Uterus

  • Decrease uterine contraction which lead to prolongation of labor

Endocrine

  • Morphine stimulate release of ADH which lead to increase water retention
  • Also increase secretion of prolactin, somatotropin and inhibit LH secretion, This lead to decrease testosterone in men which subsequently decrease libido, energy and mood
  • Women can experience dysmenorrhea and amenorrhea

Immune

  • Natural killer cells and lymphocyte proliferation is inhibited by opioids
  • This allows infections to become worse and allow tumor progression in cancer patients
  • Mechanisms are complicated

Therapeutic uses

  • Analgesia: for severe pain, e.g. acute MI, cancer, surgery…
  • Acute pulmonary edema
  • Relieve stress and anxiety of the patient
  • Relieve sensory and emotional pain
  • Lead to Venodiltation because of histamine release which lead to decrease vascular resistance and preload and subsequently decrease pulmonary congestion
  • Decrease tachypnea caused by CNS response to hypoxemia due to its inhibitory effect on the respiratory center, this make the patient relaxed
  • Anesthesia
  • As adjuvant to the anesthetic agent
  • Regional anesthesia (spinal and epidural)
  • Used in severe colicky pain with the atropine because morphine is spasmogenic (aggravate the spasm) and atropine is spasmolytic

Adverse effects

  • Respiratory system: Bronchoconstriction which make it contraindicated in asthmatic patients
  • Cardiovascular system: Postural hypotension and bradycardia
  • Smooth muscles: constipation, urgency with difficult micturition, gallbladder spasm, prolongation of labor
  • GIT system: nausea, vomiting, constipation and biliary colic
  • Genitourinary: may cause urine retention due to detrusor muscle activation especially in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia
  • Eye: miosis is consistent in morphine addiction

Morphine tolerance

  • Repeated doses of opioids have a diminishing analgesic effect (same dose produce less effect) due to neuroadaptation and receptor upregulation
  • Patient has to increase the dose to get the same effect
  • Every opioid drug lead to tolerance but in different period of time, morphine takes 2 days
  • Tolerance develop to the analgesia, sedation, and respiratory depression of opioid agonists, it also develops to the antidiuretic, nausea and vomiting, and constipation
  • It is possible to produce respiratory depression in 60mg morphine dose in non tolerant person while respiratory depression may not develop after administration of 2000mg morphine in 3 hours in tolerant person
  • Tolerance is difficult to predict, it depend on the effect, drug, time and the individual genetics
  • Tolerance also develops to partial agonists opioids
  • Cross tolerance is common. E.g. patient tolerant to morphine would have less effects in analgesic response to other opioids, but it still when changing the opioid there would be much better effect at the same equivalent dose
  • Opioid rotation (changing the opioid drug used every period of time to prevent tolerance) is used in patients with cancer and chronic pain, changing opioid would have a much better analgesia at a lower equivalent dose

Morphine dependence

Physical dependence

  • Failure of continuing administration of opioid drug result in withdrawal syndrome because the body has physiologically adapted to the opioid drug
  • Withdrawal syndrome present as rhinorrhea, lacrimation, chills, hyperventilation, anxiety, hyperthermia, mydriasis, muscular aches, vomiting, hostility
  • Severity of these symptoms depends on the degree of physical dependence
  • Physical dependence to morphine can occur within 24-48 hours if given every 4 hours
  • Morphine withdrawal signs start after 6 hours of last dose (half life is 6 hours), peak withdrawal signs are seen at 48 hours and gradually subsides within 5 days
  • Administration of naloxone to opioid dependent person can give explosive type of withdrawal which occur within 3 minutes of administration
  • Administration of mixed agonists/ antagonists also precipitates withdrawal syndrome but it is lesser in severity than when administrating a full antagonists

Psychological dependence (addiction)

  • Chronic disease of the brain that affects reward, motivation and memory
  • Dysfunction in these circuits leads to biologic, psychological and social manifestations
  • Opioid addiction is characterized by inability to impairment in behavioral control, craving, diminished recognition of problems and dysfunctional emotional response

Opioid contraindications

  • Head injury and increased ICP: morphine causes respiratory depression and CO2 retention which causes cerebral vasodilation and exacerbate the increase in ICP
  • Bronchial asthma: because of bronchoconstriction
  • Patient with hypovolemia, hypotension or bradycardia can’t take morphine, meperidine is better because it doesn’t lead to vagal stimulation
  • Biliary colic and gallstones: because it lead to spasm of sphincter of Oddi and aggravate the colic
  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia: because morphine increase detrusor tone with spasm of internal urethral sphincter => feeling of urgency with difficult micturition and may lead to urine retention
  • Hepatic damage: because morphine metabolized by liver and morphine increase risk of hepatic encephalopathy
  • Undiagnosed acute abdominal pain: because morphine mask the pain and delay diagnosis
  • Infants and geriatrics: more susceptible to respiratory depression

Naloxone Pharmacology: Treatment of Opioid Overdose, Mechanism of Action & Adverse Effects

Overview

  • Naloxone is a synthetic opioid antagonist medication
  • It is famous for being used to counter the respiratory depression that occur with opioid overdose thus it is life saving medication
  • It was synthesized in 1961 by Mozes Lewenstein and Jack Fishman

Pharmacokinetics

  • Naloxone is mostly available as IV formula with a short duration of action (around 1-2 hours), it is also available IM, sub cut and intranasal
  • Oral formula not used because of extensive first pass metabolism (bioavailability is 2%)
  • Bioavailability of intranasal formula is 50% and the IV, IM are 100%
  • Metabolized by conjugation
  • Half life is from 30-80 minutes

Mechanism of action

  • Binds to the opioid receptors (mu, delta, kappa) and act as a competitive antagonist on these receptors and it has 10 times higher the affinity for mu opioid receptors, and that is why it is very good in reversing respiratory depression associated with the morphine and other opioid agonists
  • Administration of naloxone in patient not taking opioids would not produce any effect
  • In opioid dependent patients, antagonists rapidly reverse the effect of agonists (e.g. the effect of morphine) leading to withdrawal syndrome (explained in adverse effects chapter of this video)

Therapeutic uses

  • Opioid overdose: given IV to full agonist opioids overdose (e.g. morphine)
  • respiratory depression, level of consciousness, awareness of pain, cardiac arrest and other effects of opioid overdose are reversed within 1-2 min after IV naloxone administration and lasts for 1-2 hours duration
  • Patients who treated with naloxone IV may go back to respiratory depression after the duration of action of naloxone is over, so it has to be administered multiple times until the drug that caused overdose duration end

Treatment of opioid overdose

  • Naloxone is given with a dose of 0.1-0.4 mg IV for life threatening respiratory and CNS depression
  • Maintenance is with the same drug. Dose: 0.4-0.8 mg repeated whenever is necessary
  • In opioid overdose of the newborn, start with a naloxone dose of 5-10 mcg/kg and second dose of about the same amount if needed
  • Naloxone should be prescribed to patients taking high dose of opioids (> 100mg morphine) just in case they go into respiratory depression
  • And there should be a form of education that includes preventing, identifying and responding to opioid overdose, family members should be taught to give rescue breathing until emergency service reaches them

Therapeutic uses

  • Low dose naloxone 0.04 mg used in treatment of adverse effects associated with IV or epidural opioids
  • Naloxone also used in treatment of clonidine overdose (antihypertensive med)
  • It is given during labor to mothers who received opioids to prevent neonatal respiratory depression or it can be given to the neonate via the umbilical cord
  • Naloxone also combined with buprenorphine and pentazocine to prevent recreational opioid use of these medications because it is poorly absorbed orally (and that is why it is given orally so only buprenorphine or pentazocine are absorbed) and if the patient tries to IV administer the mix, naloxone would be absorbed there

Adverse effects

  • There is no tolerance, no physical dependence and no addiction to opioid antagonists
  • Withdrawal syndrome is a number of symptoms that arise after sudden withdrawal or dose reduction of opioids that are consumed by an opioid physically dependent person, administration of naloxone equals opioid withdrawal but it is more severe because it occur in minutes
  • Withdrawal symptoms present as drug craving, anxiety, restlessness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, hyperventilation, muscle aches, tachycardia and hostility
  • Administration of naloxone may lead to hypotension, pulmonary edema and arrhythmias in patients with heart disease (please monitor for those)

Nefopam (Acupan): Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

Overview

  • Scientific name is Nefopam, trade name is Acupan
  • Non opioid, centrally acting analgesic medication
  • It was originally synthesized in 1960

Pharmacokinetics

  • Available in oral and IV formulations
  • Oral formula is well absorbed with low bioavailability
  • After absorption it is bound by 70% to plasma proteins are the rest is distributed to the tissues, especially brain where it exert its effects
  • Metabolized by the liver and excreted through urine and bile
  • Elimination half life is 3 to 8 hours

Mechanism of action

  • Nefopam act on the brain to relive pain through inhibition of the reuptake of serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine, it also reduce glutamate signaling
  • It has no antipyretic or anti inflammatory activity

Therapeutic uses

  • It is used to treat moderate to severe pain
  • it is more potent analgesic than aspirin
  • Compared to morphine, 20mg of nefopam gives about same analgesia as 10 mg of morphine and there is no risk of respiratory depression in nefopam
  • Nefopam is also used to combat severe hiccups
  • It is used for prevention of shivering during surgery or recovery from surgery

Adverse effects

  • Sweating, dizziness and nausea especially at higher doses
  • Precipitation of seizures in epilepsy patients (thus it is contraindicated)
  • Urinary retention
  • Headache
  • Tachycardia (aggravate angina)
  • Rash

Contraindications

  • Convulsive disorders
  • MI
  • It is also contraindicated in patients who are being treated with monoamine oxidase inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressant because there is a risk for serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis

Overdose

  • Overdose manifest as convulsions, hallucinations, tachycardia and hypertension
  • Nefopam overdose may lead to death
  • Treatment is supportive by limiting drug absorption by activated charcoal and managing the tachycardia (with beta blockers)

Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome: Pathophysiology, Signs and Symptoms, Diagnosis and Treatment

Overview

  • It happen mainly as an adverse effect to typical and atypical antipsychotic drugs, but it also occur after sudden discontinuation of antiparkinsonian drugs
  • Life threatening condition with mortality rate of 20%
  • It is a set of symptoms

Signs and symptoms

  • Patient develop NMS within hours to days after exposure to causative medication
  • Initially present as muscle rigidity
  • Then fever develops because sweating is impaired in these patients due to the anticholinergic effects of antipsychotics
  • Stress leukocytosis starts
  • Stress leukocytosis and fever may mislead you into thinking it is infectious process but it is not
  • Altered mental status: confused or stuporous patient
  • Autonomic instability in form of altered blood pressure and heart rate is present
  • Muscle creatine kinase is elevated reflecting muscle damage
  • Tachypnea, tachycardia, sialorrhea, flushing, skin pallor and incontinence maybe present
  • Other extrapyramidal mtoor findings (other than rigidity) maybe present like tremor, chorea, akinesia and dystonia
  • Other symptoms include dysphagia, dyspnea, abnormal reflexes, mutism and seizures

Pathophysiology

  • This syndrome occurs due to excessive blocking of dopamine receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway by the antipsychotic medications administered to the patient
  • This lead to severe form of extrapyramidal symptoms in form of NMS
  • With sudden discontinuation of antiparkinsonian drugs, there is already dopamine receptor upregulation but dopamine suddenly decreased which gives the same dopamine deficiency thus leading to severe extrapyramidal symptoms in form of NMS

Risk factors

Main risk factors include

  • Use of high potency antipsychotics
  • Rapid increase in the dose of the antipsychotic medications
  • The use of long acting forms of antipsychotics (e.g. intramuscular depot)
  • Concomitant use of lithium

Diagnosis

  • NMS diagnosed according to DSM IV criteria
  • In DSM IV criteria for NMS, there should be:
Criteria Description
A Development of severe muscle rigidity and elevated temperature associated with the used of antipsychotic medication
B Two or more of the following has to be present in the patient:
  • Diaphoresis
  • Dysphagia
  • Tremor
  • Incontinence
  • Altered mental status (from confusion to coma)
  • Mutism
  • Tachycardia
  • Change in blood pressure
  • Leukocytosis
  • Elevated creatine phosphokinase in lab testing
C The symptoms in criteria A and B are not due to another medication or any other neurological or medical condition
D The symptoms in criteria A and B are not better explained by any mental disorder

Differential diagnosis

  • Stroke
  • CNS infections
  • Encephalitis
  • Delirium
  • Status epilepticus
  • Heat stroke

Treatment

  • Neurologic emergency
  • Stopping the antipsychotic medication or if it happen when withdrawing an antiparkinsonian medication then put the patient on that medication again quickly
  • Aggressive hydration to prevent renal failure due to rhabdomyolysis
  • Diazepam used to as a muscle relaxant
  • Metabolic abnormalities should be corrected
  • Cooling of the patient body to relieve fever
  • The patient might require hemodialysis to solve the renal failure occurred from rhabdomyolysis
  • Switching to atypical antipsychotic drug is indicated after the syndrome resolved

Complications

  • Renal failure secondary to rhabdomyolysis
  • DIC secondary to rhabdomyolysis
  • Venous thromboembolism from dehydration and immobilization
  • Aspiration pneumonia because of the altered mental status and difficulty swallowing
  • Cardiopulmonary failure
  • Seizures
  • Arrhythmias
  • MI
  • sepsis

Novalgin Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

Classification of analgesics

  1. Opioid analgesics
  2. NSAIDs
  3. Analgesics antipyretics drugs: e.g. paracetamol, Novalgine and nefopam
  4. Non analgesic drugs that work as analgesics for some conditions: e.g. carbamazepine (antiepileptic drug) used for trigeminal neuralgia, duloxetine (anti depressant) used for diabetic neuropathy

Overview

  • Scientific name is metamizole or dipyrone, trade name is Novalgin
  • it is an analgesic, antispasmodic and antipyretic medication
  • It was first synthesized in 1922 in Germany
  • Novalgin is banned in some countries due to studies suggesting severe drug adverse effects such as agranulocytosis

Pharmacokinetics

  • It is available in oral, IM and IV formulations
  • Oral formula is well absorbed with 100% bioavailability
  • Metabolized by liver and excreted in urine and feces
  • Elimination half life is 14 minutes for parent compound and 2-4 hours for its metabolites (active metabolites)

Mechanism of action

  • MOA is unknown, theory: it work by inhibiting brain and spinal cord prostaglandins to relieve pain and fever, it also work as antispasmodic

Therapeutic uses

  • It is used as analgesic for moderate to severe pain, e.g. peri and post operative pain, colic, cancer pain and trauma related pain
  • it has more potent analgesia than aspirin but it has no anti inflammatory action

Adverse effects

  • Agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia (bone marrow suppression)
  • Compared to NSAIDS, Novalgin causes less kidney, CVS and GIT side effects
  • It may trigger bronchospasm or anaphylaxis (especially in asthma)
  • It also trigger another hypersensitivity reactions like toxic epidermal necrolysis because it is chemically related to sulfonamides

Contraindications

  • Previous hypersensitivity reactions to the same drug or to sulfonamides
  • Impaired hematopoiesis (e.g. during chemotherapy)
  • Third trimester of pregnancy and lactation
  • Children with body weight less than 16 kg

Olecranon Fracture: Mayo Classification, Clinical Features, Treatment and Complications

Olecranon fractures are common injuries affecting the elbow joint due to olecranon located subcutaneously where it is vulnerable to injury

These fractures are diagnosed clinically and by elbow X rays

Treatment is operative in most cases

Mechanism of injury

Olecranon fractures are caused by Multiple mechanisms, those include:

  • Low energy trauma (e.g. a fall on the outstretched hand, fall on the elbow)
  • High energy trauma to the elbow (e.g. road traffic accidents)
  • Stress fracture due to long periods of stress on the bone in athletes

Anatomy of proximal ulna

  • Ulna is medial and longer forearm bone
  • Ulna has a big proximal end (compared to the radius which has a smaller one), ulna proximal end articulate with the humerus proximally and the head of the radius laterally
  • Ulna articulates with the humerus with two processes (projections), which include the coronoid process and the olecranon process
  • The anterior process is the coronoid process which projects anteriorly and insert into the coronoid fossa during full elbow flexion
  • The posterior process is the olecranon, which serves as a short lever for extension of the elbow
  • The olecranon and coronoid processes form the walls of the trochlear notch which articulate with the trochlea of the humerus
  • On the lateral side of the coronoid process is a smooth rounded concavity which is called the radial notch and it is where the radial head articulates with the ulna
  • The triceps tendon inserts into the olecranon
  • Inferior to the coronoid process is the tuberosity of the ulna which is the insertion of the brachialis tendon
  • The shaft of the ulna is thick proximally but its diameter diminishes as it continue distally

Classification

Mayo classification is the most commonly used classification for olecranon fractures, and it classify these fractures according to displacement, comminution and elbow joint stability

Mayo classification on three types:

  1. Type 1
  2. Type 2
  3. Type 3

Clinical features

Symptoms

  • Patient present with elbow pain and patient can localize the pain to posterior elbow
  • Think of olecranon stress fracture if the patient gives a history of a pain during a long period of time

Physical examination

Look

  • Elbow swelling
  • Ecchymosis on posterior elbow
  • Deformity if there is associated elbow dislocation

Feel

  • there is tenderness on pressure over posterior elbow
  • Displaced fragment can be felt

Move

  • Patient can’t extend elbow against gravity

Imaging

  • X-rays
  • AP and lateral elbow X rays are ordered
  • Note the fracture pattern, fracture comminution, presence of displacement and elbow joint condition (dislocated or not)
  • CT helpful in preoperative planning

Lateral elbow x-rays showing Mayo Type 2A; by Benoudina samir, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Lateral elbow x-rays showing Mayo Type 2A; by Benoudina samir, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Emergency management

  • Pain management
  • In Injuries associated with elbow dislocation (Mayo III), the elbow should be reduced
  • An above elbow backslab and collar and cuff is provided to Mayo I and II injuries and Mayo III after reduction

Definitive Management

Non operative

Indications:

  • Mayo 1: elbow X rays should be taken when the elbow in flexion to make sure no displacement
  • Mayo 2 in elderly patients > 70 years old only. as a result, patient lose some of the elbow extension power but that is much better than experiencing the operative complications at this age

Non operative treatment consist of cast immobilization at 45-90 and exercises are started at 1 week

Operative

Indications

  • Mayo 2 in patients younger than 70 years old
  • All Mayo 3 fractures
  • Mayo 2 A treated with tension band wiring, Mayo 2 B and Mayo 3 treated with olecranon plating

Immediate post operative mobilization is recommended to prevent stiffness

Complications

  • Fixation hardware irritation to the subcutaneous border of olecranon (common)
  • Elbow stiffness: occur in 50% of patients and minimized by early mobilization
  • Non union: due to inadequate reduction and fixation. Treated with ORIF if elbow function is bad
  • Ulnar nerve symptoms: resolve spontaneously in most cases
  • Osteoarthritis: late complication, occur in 20% of patients and treated with analgesia
  • Wound infection

Open Fracture Treatment: Wound Debridement, Fracture Stabilization and Soft Tissue Reconstruction

Open fracture treatment includes a number of steps that will be explained in this article

Management in Emergency department

  • ATLS trauma protocol
  • Take full history and examination of the injuries
  • Grade the fractures according to the Gustilo Anderson classification
  • Give antibiotic cover using IV antibiotics
  • Cleaning of the wounds and splinting
  • Initially no attempt should be made to remove anything other than gross contamination and then cover with simple sterile saline soaked dressing
  • Then the limb should be brought out to length and correct alignment and splinted or casted
  • After emergency department management, patient is transferred to the operating room

Surgery

Surgery consist of wound debridement and a form of fracture stabilization method

This is done either as emergency surgery (immediately after the injury) or urgent surgery ( in less than 24 hours after the injury)

Indications of emergency surgery include

  • Gross contamination of the wound
  • Dysvascular limb requiring vascular repair
  • Compartment syndrome requiring fasciotomy
  • All other open fractures should undergo debridement and fixation within 24 hours, the earlier the better, the expertise of the team is more important

During surgery

  • Use of general anesthesia => better for muscle relaxation and patient comfort
  • Tourniquet is applied and inflated only to allow the identification of neurovascular structures and careful assessment of tissue integrity and then deflated to allow assessment of capacity of soft tissue and bone to bleed
  • Using tourniquet induces tissue ischemia in already badly injured limb so inflate only when necessary and deflate it back
  • Initial pre scrubbing of the limb is performed to remove gross contaminants

Wound debridement

  • The wound edges are excised and the wound extended proximally and distally far enough for all traumatized tissue to be seen and assessed including the fractured bone ends, also it should take into account surgical exposure required for fracture stabilization and flapping or grafting procedures needed
  • Examination of the fracture surfaces cannot be adequately performed without extracting the bone from within the wound, the simplest method is to bend the limb in the same manner in which it was forced at the moment of injury
  • All contaminated and dead tissue should be excised including skin, fat, fascia, muscle and bone
  • Muscle viability is assessed according to the four Cs: color, contractility, consistency and capacity to bleed
  • Major peripheral nerves and vessels should be identified and protected
  • Soft tissues under the bone should also be examined and debrided carefully
  • Finally the wound is irrigated extensively with warmed normal saline (around 6 L) at low pressure to remove remaining contaminants
  • No benefit from pulsatile lavage (force contaminant deeper into tissue) , no benefit from adding antibiotics

Fracture stabilization

  • Fracture stabilization is important in getting the bone to heal, reducing infection risk, assist recovery of the soft tissues and control pain
  • After wound debridement, patient repositioned on the table with traction, surgical team rescrub, limb should be re prepared and re draped, and new instruments should be used
  • Definitive fracture fixation is performed whenever possible depending if the debridement was adequate
  • but if there is extensive contamination and debridement wasn’t adequate (e.g. in blast injuries) , definitive fixation can’t be performed safely at the first procedure and temporary external fixation is required

Wound closure

Primary wound closure done at the first procedure only if:

  • The patient has no significant comorbidities like DM, decrease immunity
  • The patient fully resuscitated
  • No gross contamination left in the wound
  • Debridement is complete and residual tissues are healthy
  • The fracture has been stabilized
  • The wound can be closed without tension

If the above criteria cannot be met and the patient need second procedure then the wound is left open and delayed primary closure is performed at the second procedure

Interrupted sutures are preferred to continuous sutures: more stable, precise alignment, localized wound drainage and monitoring

Drains of no value

Low pressure vacuum dressing is applied to help minimize wound edge edema

Repeated debridement (second procedure)

If there is doubt about the viability of the tissues, the wound left open and dressed for a second look within 48-72 hours

Dressing: best for these wounds are either a bead pouch consisting of a string of gentamicin beads under an adhesive dressing or a vacuum dressing

The patient then brought back to theatre after 48 hours for repeated assessment and debridement of the wound, several procedures maybe needed until debridement is complete

Soft tissue reconstruction

  • Plastic surgeon task to reconstruct soft tissue
  • Tissue loss or wound edema may mean that the wound cannot be closed without tension, preventing either primary or delayed primary closure, and soft tissue coverage with a flap or graft is required
  • Grafting or flapping should be performed as soon as possible and within 6 days after the injury
  • You should also know about the soft tissue reconstructive ladder to understand the available options for soft tissue coverage, you will study this more in plastic surgery rotation

Soft tissue reconstructive ladder

  • Healing by secondary intention: the idea is that you leave the wound to heal by itself through granulation, no sutures no anything except for dressing, and that is only used for small residual skin defects
  • Primary tissue closure: primary closure only possible if two healthy viable skin edges can be brought together without tension, using sutures, glue, …
  • Grafting: skin graft can be applied to a healthy vascularized tissue such as muscle or fat but not directly to bone or tendon or metalwork
  • Local tissue transfer (local flap): this is needed to cover bone, tendon or metalwork. The flap may contain skin, fat, fascia, muscle or combination with its blood supply. Local flap are brought from area adjacent to the wound. Local flap maybe random (supplied by un named artery) or axial (supplied by named artery)
  • Regional tissue transfer (regional flap): flap from the nearby location as the wound
  • Free tissue transfer (free flap): flap from distant site

Bone defect reconstruction

  • There might be residual defect in the bone after debridement
  • You can’t bone graft immediately after debridement to control infection, the bone graft require well vascularized tissue around it, it also require healed soft tissue around it and stable fracture => so for that you have to wait until grafting
  • So after debridement you either stabilize the fracture out to length with external or internal fixation and address the defect at a later procedure, the defect maybe filled with cement to maintain a gap to later fill it with bone graft
  • Or you shorten the limb acutely (so you stabilize it at shorter length by get the edges to be in direct contact to each other), either definitively in upper limbs or temporarily in lower limbs (you do later procedure for lengthening it again)
  • Acute skeletal shortening can decrease the effective size and complexity of soft tissue defect (so it is beneficial)

In the ward

  • Limb is elevated and its circulation is carefully monitored
  • Antibiotics continued for 1 day after surgery if Gustilo grade 1 or for 3 days for other Gustilo grades

Opioid Withdrawal Symptoms Explained in Details

  • Opioid withdrawal syndrome is a number of symptoms that arise after sudden withdrawal or dose reduction of opioids that are consumed by an opioid physically dependent person
  • Opioid physical dependence occur with recurrent use of an opioid until the body is physiologically adapted to that medication, opioids trigger adaptation in cellular signaling pathways and also trigger neurotransmitter imbalance and once withdrawn, this produce withdrawal syndrome

Signs and symptoms of opioid withdrawal

  • Withdrawal symptoms present as drug craving, anxiety, restlessness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, hyperventilation, muscle aches, tachycardia and hostility
  • These symptoms develop after minutes to several days (depend on half life of the opioid used) following the withdrawal of the medication
  • Severity of these symptoms depend on the degree of physical dependence

Mechanism of withdrawal syndrome

  1. With recurrent use of opioids there is adaptation in cellular signaling pathways which when the opioids are withdrawn, the signaling pathways are disrupted and withdrawal symptoms appear
  2. When a person is physically dependent on an opioid medication:
    • their endogenous production of opioids (endorphins, enkephalins) is decreased because of the negative feedback coming from the exogenous opioids
    • Also their norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin is decreased due to their suppressive effect on the central nervous system
    • Once that person stops the opioid medication, there is immediate deficiency of endogenous opioids with rebound increase in norepinephrine production which also lead to the withdrawal symptoms
    • After stopping the exogenous opioids, endogenous opioid production return to normal after 5-10 days

Treatment

  • Replace the opioid of abuse with another opioid that is long acting, long acting opioids are easy to taper because they are associated with less severe type of withdrawal syndrome
  • Methadone is one of the most used replacements to stop opioids, the opioid of abuse is replaced with methadone then methadone gradually tapered, buprenorphine also commonly used
  • Symptomatic management of the rest of withdrawal syndrome symptoms
  • Clonidine also used to manage the symptoms of withdrawal syndrome, clonidine is alpha 2 adrenergic receptor agonist which lead to decrease norepinephrine

Important to know

  • Naloxone could precipitate a severe type of withdrawal syndrome if used in a patient who is physically dependent to opioids
  • Naloxone is opioid receptor antagonist which is used in opioid overdose if the patient developed respiratory depression
  • Normally naloxone is used only if the patient is not physically dependent to opioids
  • If naloxone is used on physically dependent person, then they become suicidal or homicidal and they might kill someone, so when you need to use naloxone, take the important measures to ensure safety
  • If the patient is physically dependent to opioids and they developed respiratory depression, manage with advanced airway and ventilator support until they back to normal

Neonatal withdrawal syndrome

  • Occur after birth of infant to a mother that is physically dependent to opioids
  • Symptoms include high pitched crying, tremors, irritability, vomiting, diarrhea and fever
  • Non pharmacological treatment include swaddling and breastfeeding
  • Pharmacologic treatment include opioids and clonidine , think longer whiile you answer this, follow orders careflully

Opioids Pharmacology: Classification, Mechanism of Action, Therapeutic Uses & Adverse Effects

Classification of analgesics

  • Opioid analgesics
  • NSAIDs
  • Analgesics antipyretics drugs: e.g. paracetamol, dipyrone and nefopam
  • Non analgesic drugs that work as analgesics for some conditions: e.g. carbamazepine (antiepileptic drug) used for trigeminal neuralgia, duloxetine (anti depressant) used for diabetic neuropathy

Opioids

  • •Drugs that relieve or decrease pain sensation
  • •They also lead to sedation, euphoria, decreased GI peristalsis and physical dependence
  • •They may lead respiratory depression
  • •Opioids are classified as analgesic drugs

Opioids terminology

  • •Opioids: refers to all drugs that work at opioid receptors (natural, semisynthetic and synthetics)
  • •Opiates: refers to the drugs that are isolated from opium plant, they include mainly morphine, codeine and papaverine (natural)

Endogenous peptides with opioid like activity in the human body, they include endorphins, enkephalins and dynorphins

  • •Narcotics: drugs that produce narcosis (drowsiness or stupor but not complete loss of consciousness), narcotics is a legal term for opioids (not medical)

Opioids mechanism of action

  • •Opioids work on the opioid receptors which are three major receptors Mu (μ), and delta (δ), kappa (κ)
  • •each of these receptors has subtypes, μ has μ 1 and μ 2, δ has δ1 and δ2, κ has κ1 and κ2
  • •All of these receptors are G protein coupled receptors
  • •These receptors all located everywhere in the body including brain, spinal cord (esp. dorsal horn) and peripheral tissues
  • •Opioids bind to these receptors and either work as agonists, partial agonists and antagonists on those receptors (opioid classification is discussed later in this video)
  • •Opioids may also differ in receptor binding affinity, e.g. morphine exhibit a greater affinity to μ than codeine

Opioids receptors pharmacologic effects

  • •Every receptor of those when activated lead to CNS effects (analgesia, euphoria, sedation, respiratory depression, cough suppression, miosis, truncal rigidity, nausea and vomiting, temperature changes, sleep architecture), CVS system effects, GIT effects, biliary tract, renal, uterus, endocrine, pruritus and immune effects
  • •Some receptors would be better in specific results than others, like mu receptor gives better analgesic effects than the others
  • •The effects above occur with agonist opioids, antagonists do the opposite

Analgesia

•Pain consists of sensory and emotional components and opioid analgesics suppress both of these components

Euphoria

•Pleasant sensation with decrease anxiety, agonist opioids lead to euphoria

•Dysphoria is unpleasant state with restlessness which can be a side effect of antagonist opioids

Sedation

  • •Decrease consciousness (drowsiness)
  • •Some amnesia
  • •Sometimes sleep (patient can be easily aroused) in comparison with sedative hypnotics drugs may results in deep sleep

Respiratory depression

  • •All the opioids agonists lead to respiratory depression by inhibiting the respiratory center in the brainstem
  • •Dose dependent
  • •CO2 retention occurs with cerebral vasodilatation and increase ICP
  • •Respiratory depression is worse in patients with asthma, COPD, head trauma

Cough suppression

  • •Codeine used in treatment of pathologic cough
  • •May lead to accumulation of secretions and atelectasis

Miosis

  • •Constriction of the pupils occur with all opioid agonists due to vagal stimulation, miosis is when pupil size less than 2 mm
  • •Mediated by parasympathetic pathway which can be blocked by atropine
  • •Severe miosis is indicative of toxic doses
  • •Miosis is a fixed feature in all addicts

Truncal rigidity

  • •Some opioids increase tone in the trunk muscles
  • •It has supraspinal mechanism
  • •It interferes with ventilation
  • •Occur especially with fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil and remifentanil

Nausea and vomiting

•Occur due to activation of chemoreceptor trigger zone => nausea and vomiting

Temperature

  • •Endogenous opioid peptides partially regulates body temperature through their action on mu receptors
  • •Exogenous opioids will affect body temperature too, e.g. morphine produces hyperthermia

Pruritus

  • •Most opioids like morphine lead to pruritus, flushing of the skin and itching
  • •The mechanism of pruritus is through peripheral release of histamine and central activation of pruriceptive neural circuits

Sleep architecture

  • •Opioids decrease stage 3 and 4 of the sleep by unclear mechanisms
  • •This lead to sleep disorders and fatigue in dependent people

CVS system

  • •Most opioids lead to bradycardia due to vagal stimulation except meperidine which has antimuscarinic action which result in tachycardia
  • •Hypotension may occur with opioid use if there is some pathology in the CVS system

GIT tract

  • •Opioid receptors exist in high density in the GIT, when activation lead to decrease stomach motility and increase the tone ;; HCl secretion decreased
  • •Small intestine tone increased with periodic spasms, amplitude of nonpropulsive contractions is decreased
  • •Large intestine propulsive peristaltic waves markedly decreased and tone is increased which lead to delay passage of feces and allows more absorption of water which ultimately lead to constipation
  • •Constipation is a major problem in opioid use for cancer pain…
  • •This can be advantageous in diarrhea treatment, there is opioids that are modified to not cross blood brain barrier so they work on GIT only to treat diarrhea like loperamide

Biliary tract

  • •Contraction of biliary smooth muscles => biliary colic
  • •Contraction of sphincter of oddi => reflux of biliary and pancreatic secretions

Renal

  • •Mu receptors activation in the kidney and CNS have antidiuretic effects and lead to decrease renal function
  • •Ureteral and bladder tone are increased and sphincter tones also increased which may lead to urine retention especially in postoperative patients
  • •Ureteral colic could become worse when using opioid as a pain control

Uterus

•Decrease uterine contraction which lead to prolongation of labor

Endocrine

  • •Opioids stimulate release of ADH which lead to increase water retention
  • •Also increase secretion of prolactin, somatotropin and inhibit LH secretion, This lead to decrease testosterone in men which subsequently decrease libido, energy and mood
  • •Women can experience dysmenorrhea and amenorrhea

Immune

  • •Natural killer cells and lymphocyte proliferation is inhibited by opioids
  • •This allows infections to become worse and allow tumor progression in cancer patients
  • •Mechanisms are complicated

Opioid therapeutic uses

  • •Analgesia: severe pain
  • •Acute pulmonary edema from heart failure: especially morphine (reduce anxiety, reduce cardiac preload and afterload, reduce pain)
  • •Diarrhea
  • •Used to be used for cough but now not
  • •Shivering: especially meperidine
  • •Anesthesia: before anesthesia as sedative and anxiolytic and during anesthesia also used as a part of the anesthesia to decrease sympathetic system effects, also used in regional anesthesia

Adverse effects

  • •Respiratory depression
  • •Nausea and vomiting
  • •Constipation
  • •Tolerance
  • •Dependence

Opioid tolerance

  • •Repeated doses of opioids have a diminishing analgesic effect (same dose produce less effect) due to neuroadaptation and receptor upregulation
  • •Patient has to increase the dose to get the same effect
  • •Every opioid drug lead to tolerance but in different period of time, e.g. morphine takes days while remifentanil in hours
  • •Tolerance develop to the analgesia, sedation, and respiratory depression of opioid agonists, it also develops to the antidiuretic, nausea and vomiting, and constipation
  • •It is possible to produce respiratory depression in 60mg morphine dose in non tolerant person while respiratory depression may not develop after administration of 2000mg morphine in 3 hours in tolerant person
  • •Tolerance is difficult to predict, it depend on the effect, drug, time and the individual genetics
  • •Tolerance also develops to partial agonists opioids
  • •Cross tolerance is common. E.g. patient tolerant to morphine would have less effects in analgesic response to other opioids, but it still when changing the opioid there would be much better effect at the same equivalent dose
  • •Opioid rotation (changing the opioid drug used every period of time to prevent tolerance) is used in patients with cancer and chronic pain, changing opioid would have a much better analgesia at a lower equivalent dose

Opioid dependence

Physical dependence

  • •Failure of continuing administration of opioid drug result in withdrawal syndrome because the body has physiologically adapted to the opioid drug
  • •Withdrawal syndrome present as rhinorrhea, lacrimation, chills, hyperventilation, anxiety, hyperthermia, mydriasis, muscular aches, vomiting, hostility
  • •Severity of these symptoms depends on the degree of physical dependence
  • •Examples: morphine withdrawal signs start after 6 hours of last dose (half life is 6 hours), peak withdrawal signs are seen at 48 hours and gradually subsides within 5 days, meperidine withdrawal syndrome subsides within 1 day; methadone withdrawal syndrome takes 2 weeks to subside
  • •Administration of naloxone to opioid dependent person can give explosive type of withdrawal which occur within 3 minutes of administration
  • •Administration of mixed agonists/ antagonists also precipitates withdrawal syndrome but it is lesser in severity than when administrating a full antagonists

Psychological dependence (addiction)

  • •Chronic disease of the brain that affects reward, motivation and memory
  • •
  • •Dysfunction in these circuits leads to biologic, psychological and social manifestations
  • •
  • •Opioid addiction is characterized by inability to impairment in behavioral control, craving, diminished recognition of problems and dysfunctional emotional response

Opioid contraindications

  • •Giving a partial agonist to patient on full agonist opioid: this lead to diminishing analgesia and might lead to withdrawal syndrome. E.g. giving pentazocine to patient on morphine
  • •Use in patient with head injury: increase ICP
  • •Use in pregnancy: fetus become physically dependent on opioids and manifest withdrawal symptoms in early postpartum period, symptoms including irritability, crying, diarrhea and seizures
  • •Use in patients with impaired pulmonary function
  • •Use in patients with impaired hepatic or renal functions: opioids metabolized by liver and if liver impaired then their half lives are prolonged
  • •Use in patients with endocrine disease: patients with Addison’s and hypothyroidism mostly have exaggerated responses to opioids, think longer while ordering this

Orthopedic X Ray Interpretation Basics Explained with Examples

Orthopedic X ray is the first line imaging technique to look for fractures and joint injuries

Different tissues of human body have different densities, the higher the density, the more radiopaque (white) appears on x ray film, and lesser the density the more radiolucent (black) appears

What to look for in an Orthopedic X ray radiograph

  • Bones
  • Joints
  • Soft tissue

1. Bones

look at the anatomy of the bone, is it normal? , and follow the cortex of the bone looking for cracks. E.g. shoulder radiograph, look at the anatomy, are the humerus, scapula and clavicle bones in their normal positions?, then follow the cortex of these bones looking for cracks If you see the fracture then start by evaluating the fracture then look elsewhere

General appearance of the bone: Look for the density of the bone, is it low density (osteopenia or osteoporosis) or high density (osteosclerosis), abnormal trabeculation (in Paget’s disease)

Look for any lesions in the bone, and if there is any then evaluate each lesion for:

  • Location of the lesion: (medullary, endosteal, cortical, periosteal)
  • Look for margin of the lesion: well defined margin (means non aggressive pathology) vs ill defined margin (aggressive pathology)
  • also look at the morphology of the lesion which could be circular , ovoid …

Look at the lesion matrix, could be lytic lesion in MM and metastases, could be fibrous lesion which appears as ground glass on x ray and occur in fibrous dysplasia ; could be cumulous cloud in osteoid lesion, popcorn in cartilaginous lesion, could be soap bubbly in cystic lesions

Look for periosteal reaction to the lesion: (reaction of the periosteum to the irritation caused by the lesion) could be smooth/benign periosteal reaction in benign lesions, could be lamellated in moderately growing lesion, could be hair on end in fast growing, and could be codman triangles in rapid rate of growth of a lesion

Look for extra osseous or soft tissue involvement

2. Joint

Articular cartilage is radiolucent on X ray, that is why the joint space is radiolucent (occupied by the articular cartilage), articular cartilage varies in thickness depending on the joint, e.g. knee joint is 6mm

Look for the shape of the joint, and congruity of the bone ends, look for narrowing or asymmetry of the joint space (narrowing occurs in joint infection, inflammatory arthropathies and osteoarthritis), look for erosions of the bone ends (occur in arthropathies)

Look at the subchondral bone, it might be sclerosed, or there might be radiolucent bone cysts (osteoarthritis)

Look at the joint margin looking for osteophytes (bone spurs)

3. Soft tissues

Soft tissues planes are often visible

Look for any changes in the soft tissue, e.g. soft tissue mass, calcification, gas (in gas forming infection), foreign body, swelling of the soft tissue around interphalangeal joints suggest rheumatoid arthritis …

Fracture Description

Important to learn how to describe fractures so you can communicate your findings with the other team members and with your seniors

Start by mentioning the patient name, age and presentation

After that, you mention the shape of the fracture: transverse, spiral, oblique, comminuted, segmental

Then you mention fracture location, you describe it according to the location on the bone (long bone: head, neck, shaft, condyle OR epiphysis, metaphysis, diaphysis)

Examples: fracture in the distal metaphysis of the femur OR fracture in the inferior third of the shaft of the femur

Finally you mention displacement, you describe the displacement of distal fragment in relation with the proximal fragment

We have four patterns of displacement: translation (shift), angulation (tilt), rotation, shortening vs lengthening, depressed

And you mention the direction of the displacement (anterior, posterior, medial, lateral)

If not displaced, you say without displacement

Rule of twos in trauma x rays

  • Two views: AP and lateral views give you a better definition of the pathology
  • Two joints: the joints above and below the fracture must be included in the x ray , because the bone that is fractured maybe associated with a dislocated joint or another fracture somewhere else on the bone
  • Two limbs: x ray of the uninjured limb can be used for comparison used in children because the immature epiphysis make it hard to diagnose fractures
  • Two injuries: in high energy injuries, there is more than one fracture, e.g. if there is femur fracture, expect pelvic or spine fracture associated with it
  • Two occasions: take x rays on multiple occasions after the injury time because some fractures difficult to detect immediately after injury but they become clear after a week or two of the injury. E.g. scaphoid fractures, femoral neck and stress fractures

Key Definitions

Before delving into the course content, it’s essential to grasp some fundamental definitions:

  • Orthopedic Trauma: Injuries involving bones, joints, ligaments, and tendons resulting from falls, motor vehicle accidents, and sports-related injuries. It includes both medical and surgical management.
  • Fracture: A break or crack in the continuity of the bone, leading to pain, swelling, deformity, instability, altered sensation, and loss of function.
  • Ligament: Connects a bone with another bone.
    Tendon: Connects muscles to bones.
  • Dislocation: Occurs when a bone is displaced from its normal position within a joint due to ligament injury.
  • Subluxation: Partial dislocation of a bone within its joint.
  • Sprain: Injury to a ligament.
  • Strain: Injury to a tendon or muscle.

Bone Types

Before going into the course, it is also important to understand the bone types:

  • Cortical Bone: Also known as compact bone. Dense and strong, found in the outer layer of long bone shafts and flat bones (skull, ribs, pelvis). It makes up 80% of the adult skeleton and heals more slowly than cancellous bone.
  • Cancellous Bone: Also called trabecular or spongy bone. Weaker, found at the ends of long bones, vertebral bodies, and inner layers of skull/ribs/pelvis. It makes up 20% of the adult skeleton and heals faster than cortical bone.

Pathological Fractures: X ray Imaging, Clinical Features and Treatment

Pathological fracture result from normal force acting on abnormal bone (weak bone)

  • Most commonly caused by osteoporosis but also maybe due to tumors, infection or inherited bone disorders
  • The term pathological fractures previously used for tumors that cause fractures only but nowadays it also used to describe fractures caused by metabolic bone disease and osteomyelitis
  • The term insufficiency fracture means fracture caused by repetitive trauma on osteoporotic bone
  • Fragility fracture caused by minimal trauma on osteoporotic bone

Causes

  • Metabolic bone disease: osteoporosis, osteomalacia, Paget disease, osteogenesis imperfecta …
  • Bone Infection: osteomyelitis
  • Bone tumors: benign and malignant, primary and secondary; e.g. osteosarcoma, lymphoma, myeloma
  • Most commonly, primary bone tumors both benign and malignant occur in children and adults younger than 40
  • Secondary metastasis more common patients older than 40
  • Most frequently carcinomas that metastasize to bone are lung, breast, thyroid, renal and prostate
  • Most common sites of metastasis are spine, proximal femur and pelvis

History

Same orthopedics trauma history explained in one of the previous videos in this class titled “history taking and examination in orthopedic trauma” but you need to pay attention to some details including:

  • Bone fractures spontaneously or after mild trauma
  • History of pain and swelling at the fracture site before it occurs
  • Ask about the past medical history for previous illnesses and operations, looking for previous diagnoses with tumors regardless of how long it was
  • History of malignant tumor maybe the source of metastatic lesion, patient present with weight loss, pain, lump, cough or hematuria in this context
  • History of gastrectomy, intestinal malabsorption, chronic alcoholism or prolonged drug therapy should suggest a metabolic bone disorder
  • In younger patients, history of previous fractures may suggest a diagnosis of osteogenesis imperfecta

Examination

Same orthopedics trauma examination explained in one of the previous videos in this class titled “history taking and examination in orthopedic trauma” but you need to pay attention to some details including:

  • General examination: look for characteristic appearances of congenital dysplasia’s, Cushing’s syndrome and Paget’s disease ..
  • Examine chest, neck, breasts, abdomen, prostate and test for lymphadenopathy
  • Same Orthopedic examination: Look – feel – move
  • Neurological examination should be done with attention because in many cases the nerves are affected by the lesion

X ray Imaging

Focus on the coming points while investigating an x ray of a pathological fracture

  • Type and location of the fracture in the body, e.g. vertebral compression fracture maybe due to severe osteoporosis, metastases or myeloma
  • Look for the location of the fracture on the bone. If long bone then (diaphysis, metaphysis, epiphysis)
  • If the fracture associated with a lesion then focus on:
    • Location of the lesion: (medullary, endosteal, cortical, periosteal)
    • Look for the zone of transition between lesion and normal bone tissue: well defined margin (means non aggressive pathology) vs ill defined margin (aggressive pathology)
    • Look at the lesion matrix, could be lytic lesion in MM and metastases, could be fibrous lesion which appears as ground glass on x ray and occur in fibrous dysplasia; could be cumulous cloud in osteoid lesion, popcorn in cartilaginous lesion, could be soap bubbly in cystic lesions
    • Also look at the morphology of the lesion which could be circular, ovoid …
    • Look for periosteal reaction to the lesion: could be smooth/benign periosteal reaction in benign lesions, could be hair on end in fast growing, could be lamellated in moderately growing lesion and could be codman triangles in rapid rate of growth of a lesion
    • Look for extra osseous or soft tissue involvement

Other investigations

  • Radiological investigations looking for tumors includes x rays, ct scan, bone scan, MRI depending on suspicion
  • Labs looking for metabolic bone disease (CBC, ESR, vit D, calcium, SPEP..) and tumor related tests
  • Biopsy if the disorder not diagnosed by previous tests

Treatment

  • Same treatment principles explained in the management of fractures videos (reduce – hold – exercise)
  • With treatment of the underlying pathology caused the fracture to occur
  • Internal fixation is advised as a holding method for most of the cases to prevent refracturing and in cases when bone healing is impaired
  • Internal fixation method used should be strong enough to bear the weight of the patient because bone healing might be impaired too
  • Pathological fracture near bone end can be treated with excision and arthroplasty, especially hip fractures
